blocks.text: Kinetic theory finds the pressure of an ideal gas from the random thermal motion of its molecules. For a very large number of molecules we use statistical physics, the branch of physics that uses probability theory. In this picture the atoms and molecules of a system may occupy different energy states (levels) E1, E2, E3 and so on, because they have different speeds.

blocks.title: Boltzmann distribution law
blocks.text: For two energy levels E1 (lower) and E2 (higher), the populations N1 and N2 are related by N2/N1 = e^(-dE/kB T) (13.19), where dE = E2 - E1. The factor e^(-dE/kB T) is the Boltzmann factor. The probability of finding a molecule in a given energy state falls exponentially as the energy divided by kB T increases, so more particles are in lower energy states than in higher ones.

In a gas container a molecule undergoes billions of collisions every second. Each collision changes its speed and so its kinetic energy, but kinetic theory shows that the average kinetic energy at temperature T is Eav = (3/2) kB T (13.20), where kB is in effect the gas constant per molecule. The ideal gas model is the base from which statistical mechanics grew; with modifications it also explains 'non-ideal' gases, such as the hot, dense gas inside stars (topic 13.6).

blocks.title: For your information
blocks.text: In 1860 James Clerk Maxwell (1831-1879) derived an expression for the distribution of molecular speeds in a system at thermal equilibrium. About 60 years later, experiments confirmed Maxwell's predictions.
